rv.q: "Other Desert Cities" is a resounding piece of theater, not simply because of the subject matter but because of the performances.
I had a blast at director John Benjamin Hickey's pulsing, potent, gilded age production.

Ms. Louis-Dreyfus gives a performance that shimmers with wit throughout, making a confident Broadway debut, even if her innate flair for comedy sometimes threatens to obscure the shadows that trail her character.
A decade and a half after its premiere, this revival makes a strong case for its ranking among the better of those, and a definitive one for its dissection of American rot.
There's no doubt that we want to follow this cast wherever it asks us to go, even when that's a pretty big ask.
To be clear, is a sometimes clever family drama, staged handsomely, but not brilliantly.
But the likeable enough Broadway revival of Jon Robin Baitz’s sharp-tongued drama, which opened Sunday night at the Hudson Theatre, takes these people’s competing personalities way too far.
But the fire in the hearth of Scott Pask's elegant set provides more real heat than most of the production.
This Other Desert Cities, directed by John Benjamin Hickey, is wobbly from the start, off-rhythm and woefully imbalanced in its performances.
If only these actors could dedicate themselves to material more worthy of all our time.

Under John Benjamin Hickey’s deft direction, a stellar five-person ensemble made up of Louis-Dreyfus, Allison Janney, Ed Harris, Lily Rabe and Joe Keery brings humor, humanity and devastating emotional depth to a crackling revival that feels strikingly relevant in 2026.
But Other Desert Cities also features sympathetic, complex characters who largely defy our expectations, with the result that it's consistently engrossing nonetheless.
When Harris looks at her, registering his disappointment—'I only had a little bit of my heart left intact after we lost Henry, and what's left is breaking'—your heart will break too.
There's really nothing else to say other than the Seinfeld alum steals the show from the second the action begins, making her Broadway debut a rousing success.
It's a first-rate production, in many ways better than the original. But a revisit of Other Desert Cities, even one as beautifully rendered as this, reveals the play's limitations.
It speaks to the power of Baitz's play that the core tragedy works brilliantly with two such different interpretations of Polly Wyeth.
Rabe is consistently mesmerizing, proving why Brooke is the true fulcrum of this unbalanced tale.
The deftness of Baitz's dramatic construction offsets, here, a merely serviceable staging by director John Benjamin Hickey for this revival.
But most of the memorable moments in the production belong to other cast members.
But look beyond its provocative mirage, and this arid production will leave you thirsting for more.
Real or not, it ultimately has more spark than the actors around it.
But a revival needs more than an impressive guest list, and this production never makes a convincing case that 'Other Desert Cities' needed another trip to Broadway.
Alas, despite Baitz’s well-made play and an A-list cast, this revival is under-directed by John Benjamin Hickey, which leaves the actors feeling unmoored.
Other Desert Cities, at least in this constellation of performances, doesn't offer a coherent point of view on the Wyeths' solipsistic privilege.
Funny, formidable, and fiercely human, Louis-Dreyfus unfurls a mother whose love can be as devastating as the secrets she protects.
Despite all the squabbling and acting out, family values still hold sway.

cn.t: A starry cast led by Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Ed Harris elevates this timely revival of Baitz's family drama, though critics are divided on whether the 2011 play still resonates, with some finding it riveting and others seeing dated theatrics.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored 1903 gem — one of the most gorgeous small theaters on Broadway. The 2017 renovation delivered some of the widest and most comfortable seats in the Theater District, with excellent sightlines from the intimate 970-seat house.

vr.q: Don't miss your chance to see this cast go toe to toe on a Broadway stage.
